newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Heavy bank withdrawals send Pakistan rates up.
newsitem.headline: Heavy bank withdrawals send Pakistan rates up.

text.p: Large-scale withdrawals from banks caused by a loss of confidence in the economy have sent Pakistani money rates and yields on six-month federal bonds soaring, financial market dealers said on Tuesday.
"The liquidity crunch is the result of heavy withdrawals from bank deposits as investor confidence has ebbed during the past few weeks," dealer Salman Baig at KASB & Co said.

Political uncertainty, bad economic figures, the International Monetary Fund's delay in paying instalments of a $600 million standby loan and a possible downgrading of Pakistan's credit rating had undermined investor confidence, one banker said.

With interbank rates for overnight and one-week funds soaring to 17 percent and above, banks were approaching the discounting window of the State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) to square their positions, Baig said.
"Banks are discounting six to eight billion rupees ($162 to $216 million) daily since last week, which is a record and shows the amount by which the market is short," he added.

Baig said Monday's auction of six-month federal bonds, at which the SBP accepted only 53.225 million rupees in bids at a weighted average of 13.6406 percent a year, showed that the central bank itself was running short of funds.
"The higher yield at which the bids were accepted shows the central bank was itself in dire need of funds," Baig said.
The central bank had set a pre-auction target of 4.089 billion rupees, but received bids worth a total of 353.225 million rupees out of which 53.225 million were accepted.
Dealers said the highest bids offered to the central bank were at 14.25 percent.
In the previous auction held on September 17, bids worth 50 million rupees were accepted at a weighted average annual yield of 13.4995 percent.
Dealers said the shortage of funds was so acute that banks feared the SBP might start refusing to discount.

A foreign banker, who asked not to be identified, said the withdrawal of $200 million to $300 million from foreign exchange deposits in the past few weeks had aggravated the normal scarcity of funds at the end of the July-September quarter.
"The banks themselves are so jittery at the moment that even higher yields offered by the central bank on federal bonds may not move them to bring in funds from abroad," the banker said.
Foreign banks usually bring institutional funds from abroad in foreign currency and swap them for rupees with the SBP.
Bankers said the shortage of funds in the interbank market could squeeze funding for the corporate sector, whose demand for advances usually picks up in the October-December quarter.
"This could mean a slowdown of the economy in the short term," one dealer said.
